an3.86:1.1: _Kulaputta_ (literally, “son of a family”) typically refers to someone from a well-to-do or respected family, a “gentleman”. It is a gendered term which assumes the social status of men. | For _attakāma_ as “who desire self-knowledge” see [mn31:3.5]() and note.
an3.86:2.1: “Limited immersion and wisdom” means they have partially devloped the jhānas and insight. It does not mean they are entirely bereft of both.
an3.86:2.2: The “lesser and minor training rules” are not defined, and the senior monks at the First Council were unable to agree on them ([pli-tv-kd21:1.9.3]()). Nonetheless, the Pali Vinaya consistently labels the 92 Pācittiya rules as “lesser” (_khuddaka_; [pli-tv-bu-vb-pc92:2.2.22](), [pli-tv-bi-vb-pc96:2.2.22](), [pli-tv-pvr1.1:219.3]()), which would make the 4 Pātidesanīyas “minor” (_anukhuddaka_, literally “after the lesser”). The Sekhiya rules are also “minor”, but, as is clear from the mention of “150 training rules” at the start of this Sutta, they were not at this point reckoned among the training rules for recitation. | The Pācittiyas and Pātidesanīyas include anything from important moral precepts such as lying to rules against eavesdropping or applying too much plaster on a building. In each case they may be expiated by a simple confession to another monk. A related set of 30 Nissaggiya Pācittiya require in addition the relinquishment of some material object such as a robe, money, etc. Further, there are 13 Saṅghādisesa rules from which one can be restored through a lengthy process involving a large Saṅgha, but these are not “lesser”. Finally there are 4 Pārajika rules from which one can never be restored.
an3.86:6.2: While anyone can break a minor rule, what matters is a practitioners sincerity and willingness to be honest and move forward.
